title: A Unified Theoretical Model for Hysteretic Soil Freezing‐Thawing Characteristic Curves in Saline Soils: Model Development, Experimental Validation, and Simulation
content:
Abstract

Soil freezing-thawing characteristic curve (SFTCC) is crucial for cold region engineering and hydrological simulations. Most existing hydrothermal models simplify thawing as an inverse freezing process, neglecting the hysteresis effect during freeze-thaw cycles (FTC). This limitation leads to errors in predicting unfrozen water content (UWC) and initial freezing point (IFP), particularly in saline soils where solute alter ice nucleation energy barriers. This study established a novel model for the freeze-thaw hysteresis of saline soils. The framework extends traditional Gibbs-Thomson-based IFP models by integrating heterogeneous nucleation theory and solute effects. Based on a probabilistic ice formation model, the nucleation contact angle is inversely solved and coupled with the generalized Clapeyron equation and water film theory to predict UWC throughout complete FTC. Validation across 205 sets of IFP data and 30 sets of UWC data showed excellent agreement between predicted and experimental values (mean R 2 = 0.9551). Mechanistic analysis shows the IFP sensitivity to salinity varies by salt type due to eutectic properties, with NaCl-salinized soils higher sensitive than NaHCO3 and Na2SO4 salinized soils. Furthermore, SFTCC hysteresis intensifies with increasing freezing contact angle and soil particle shape factor, highlighting the dominance of nucleation energy barriers and pore size in phase transition pathways. UWC also affects SFTCC patterns by regulating effective solute concentration. Finally, the hydrothermal model was applied to simulate uniaxial freeze-thaw processes. This study elucidates the physical mechanisms underlying freeze-thaw hysteresis in saline soils. The unified model offers a physically meaningful constitutive relationship for simulating coupled water-heat-force processes in cold-region soils.
